claims.text: The coating is a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy deposited on a conventional metal substrate.
The coating's grain size governs its overall wear resistance during high-temperature sliding.
The coating's grain size governs its microscopic deformation during high-temperature sliding.
Formation of a stable oxide layer governs the coating's wear resistance during high-temperature sliding.
Formation of a stable oxide layer governs the coating's microscopic deformation during high-temperature sliding.
Temperature-dependent elemental diffusion changes the coating microstructure.
Temperature-dependent elemental diffusion promotes formation of a stable oxide layer.
Increasing the sliding temperature from approximately 500°C to 700°C increases elemental diffusion.
The increased diffusion caused by higher temperature decreases the coating grain size.
Increasing sliding temperature increases formation of a stable oxide layer.
The predicted grain-size decrease and increased stable-oxide formation improve wear resistance.
Increasing sliding temperature may increase microscopic deformation.
The proposed predictions are intended to hold from 500°C to 800°C at sliding speeds of 0.1–1 m/s, loads of 10–100 N, and durations of 100–1000 cycles.
A controlled test can vary sliding temperature while holding the other sliding conditions constant.
Failure of wear and deformation to change with temperature, or failure of grain size and oxide formation to correlate with those outcomes, would falsify the hypothesis.
